 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Male Athletes","Female Athletes","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A retrospective observational study of 36 patients admitted to an ICU after heat illness following high-intensity exercise (35 male, 1 female; mean age 22.1 years), split into a good-prognosis group (under 7 days, n=22) and a poor-prognosis group (7 days or more, n=14). Blood lactate fell significantly by 2 h and 6 h in the good-prognosis group, while in the poor-prognosis group it fell only by 6 h; at 2 h, lactate was 1.2 +/- 0.5 mmol/L (good) versus 4.2 +/- 1.2 mmol/L (poor). The 2-h lactate clearance rate was higher in the good-prognosis group (P < 0.05) and was the only lactate-clearance variable retained as a predictor in logistic regression (P = 0.041).",
 "screeningLimitations":"Single-centre retrospective study of 36 patients with 14 in the poor-prognosis group, so estimates are imprecise. The 45.5% clearance cut-off was derived in the same sample and is not validated, and the sample is hospitalised patients rather than athletes sampled for performance or health monitoring.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the 2-h clearance rate as a validated triage tool for all heat-stressed athletes, when it was derived from 36 hospitalised cases and needs external validation.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Yu L, Dong X, Li H, Mi L. The value of blood lactate and lactate clearance rate in evaluating the prognosis of athletes with heat illness of varying degrees after high-intensity exercise. BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2025;17:7.",
   "doi":"10.1186/s13102-024-01042-w",
   "abstract":"In a retrospective study of 36 athletes hospitalised with heat illness after high-intensity exercise, the authors compared blood lactate and lactate clearance between patients who recovered in under 7 days and those who took 7 days or more. Lactate was higher at admission, 2 h and 6 h in the slower-recovering group, and the 2-h clearance rate was an independent predictor of prognosis in logistic regression.",
   "tldr":"In hospitalised athletes with heat illness, lactate that stayed high and a slow 2-hour lactate clearance went with a longer hospital stay. The 45.5% clearance cut-off has not been validated outside this sample.",
   "methods":"Retrospective observational study of 36 heat-illness patients admitted to an ICU in China (December 2019 to July 2024) after high-intensity exercise. Lactate was measured at admission, 2 h and 6 h, and lactate clearance rate was calculated against admission values. Patients were grouped by prognosis (under 7 days versus 7 days or more), and groups were compared with t-tests and chi-square tests, with Pearson correlation and binary logistic regression.",
   "findings":"Lactate was lower in the good-prognosis group at admission, 2 h and 6 h (P < 0.05 or P < 0.01). At 2 h, lactate was 1.2 +/- 0.5 mmol/L versus 4.2 +/- 1.2 mmol/L, and at 6 h 0.8 +/- 0.3 versus 3.5 +/- 1.5 mmol/L. The 2-h clearance rate was higher in the good-prognosis group (P < 0.05). Admission lactate correlated with APACHE II score (r = 0.835, P < 0.01). Poor-prognosis rate was 22.2% with a 2-h clearance rate of 45.5% or more versus 55.6% below it (P < 0.05); the 6-h clearance rate was not significant.",
   "limitations":"Retrospective single-centre design with 36 patients (14 poor-prognosis), and no external validation of the 45.5% threshold. Eleven of the 14 poor-prognosis patients reached hospital more than 24 h after symptom onset, which the authors cite as a possible confounder. The abstract reports R2 = 0.83 for the LCR model, but the results give 0.835 as the correlation between lactate and APACHE II, and no model fit is reported for LCR. The text describes the sample as athletes but mostly as patients, with no exercise or performance data.",
   "practicalImplications":"Heat-illness responses for high-intensity sessions could record lactate at admission, 2 h and 6 h, so that staff can see whether lactate is clearing. The 45.5% threshold should not be used as a decision rule until it has been validated in other samples.",
   "athleteDev":"The study does not measure training, performance or adaptation, so it gives no basis for changing training prescription. Its relevance is limited to heat-illness response planning around high-intensity exercise.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its outcome is the duration of hospital stay (under 7 days versus 7 days or more), not return to play or competition."
 }
}

13	Li Yu1*, Xuehui Dong1, Huanhuan Li1 and Lili Mi2
14

16	  Abstract
17	  Background Heat stroke, a severe heat illness with organ damage, is a major cause of cause irreparable organ
18	  damage and higher death rates among military persons and athletes.
19	  Objectives To study the changes in blood lactate (Lac) levels and lactate clearance rate (LCR) in athletes with heat
20	  illness of varying degrees after high-intensity exercise and to evaluate their prognostic value.
21	  Material and methods In present study, acute care unit admitted 36 heat sickness patients following high-intensity
22	  exercise from December 2019 to July 2024, with comprehensive medical records, for retrospective study. The study
23	  population consisted of two groups of high level athletes: the favourable Prognosis Group (< 7 days, 22 cases),
24	  comprising 21 males and 1 female with a mean age of 21.8 ± 2.7 years, and the bad Prognosis Group (≥ 7 days,
25	  14cases), consisting of 14 males with a mean age of 22.6 ± 3.2 years. Lac levels were assessed at admission (0 h) and
26	  early in therapy (2 h, 6 h), and the LCR was computed. Lac and LCR values at each time point were compared between
27	  the two groups to see how they affected patient prognosis.
28	  Results After 2 and 6 h of therapy, lactate levels decreased significantly in the good prognosis group (1.2 ± 0.5
29	  mmol/L at 2 h and 0.8 ± 0.3 mmol/L at 6 h), but remained elevated in the poor prognosis group (4.2 ± 1.2 mmol/L
30	  at 2 h and 3.5 ± 1.5 mmol/L at 6 h). Core body temperature normalized in both groups, but the good prognosis
31	  group showed a more rapid decline, with temperatures of 37.4 ± 0.6 °C at 2 h and 36.8 ± 0.4 °C at 6 h in the good
32	  prognosis group, and 38.8 ± 0.8 °C at 2 h and 38.2 ± 0.9 °C at 6 h in the poor prognosis group. Notably, a significant
33	  positive correlation existed between lactate levels and APACHE II scores at admission (P < 0.01). Furthermore, logistic
34	  regression analysis revealed that the 2-hour lactate clearance rate (LCR) (R2 = 0.83) was an independent predictor of
35	  outcomes.
36	  Conclusions The study suggests that athletes with elevated lactate levels after heat illness may be at higher risk
37	  of adverse outcomes. The 2-hour lactate clearance rate (LCR) appears to be a valuable prognostic indicator, with
38	  potential applications in evaluating the severity of heat illness and guiding treatment decisions. Furthermore,

The value of blood lactate and lactate
clearance rate in evaluating the prognosis
of athletes with heat illness of varying degrees
after high-intensity exercise
Li Yu1*, Xuehui Dong1, Huanhuan Li1 and Lili Mi2


  Abstract
  Background Heat stroke, a severe heat illness with organ damage, is a major cause of cause irreparable organ
  damage and higher death rates among military persons and athletes.
  Objectives To study the changes in blood lactate (Lac) levels and lactate clearance rate (LCR) in athletes with heat
  illness of varying degrees after high-intensity exercise and to evaluate their prognostic value.
  Material and methods In present study, acute care unit admitted 36 heat sickness patients following high-intensity
  exercise from December 2019 to July 2024, with comprehensive medical records, for retrospective study. The study
  population consisted of two groups of high level athletes: the favourable Prognosis Group (< 7 days, 22 cases),
  comprising 21 males and 1 female with a mean age of 21.8 ± 2.7 years, and the bad Prognosis Group (≥ 7 days,
  14cases), consisting of 14 males with a mean age of 22.6 ± 3.2 years. Lac levels were assessed at admission (0 h) and
  early in therapy (2 h, 6 h), and the LCR was computed. Lac and LCR values at each time point were compared between
  the two groups to see how they affected patient prognosis.
  Results After 2 and 6 h of therapy, lactate levels decreased significantly in the good prognosis group (1.2 ± 0.5
  mmol/L at 2 h and 0.8 ± 0.3 mmol/L at 6 h), but remained elevated in the poor prognosis group (4.2 ± 1.2 mmol/L
  at 2 h and 3.5 ± 1.5 mmol/L at 6 h). Core body temperature normalized in both groups, but the good prognosis
  group showed a more rapid decline, with temperatures of 37.4 ± 0.6 °C at 2 h and 36.8 ± 0.4 °C at 6 h in the good
  prognosis group, and 38.8 ± 0.8 °C at 2 h and 38.2 ± 0.9 °C at 6 h in the poor prognosis group. Notably, a significant
  positive correlation existed between lactate levels and APACHE II scores at admission (P < 0.01). Furthermore, logistic
  regression analysis revealed that the 2-hour lactate clearance rate (LCR) (R2 = 0.83) was an independent predictor of
  outcomes.
  Conclusions The study suggests that athletes with elevated lactate levels after heat illness may be at higher risk
  of adverse outcomes. The 2-hour lactate clearance rate (LCR) appears to be a valuable prognostic indicator, with
  potential applications in evaluating the severity of heat illness and guiding treatment decisions. Furthermore,

15	                                     in Rugby League Match-Play

19	                                     Background: Repeated high-intensity effort (RHIE) activity is known to be a critical component of high-intensity,
20	                                     intermittent team sports. Despite the importance of this quality, there are few studies comparing the RHIE activity of higher-
21	                                     and lower-ranked teams competing in the same competition. This study characterized the distribution of recovery times
22	                                     between RHIE in Top 4 and Bottom 4 semi-elite rugby league players.
23	                                     Hypothesis: Players from Top 4 teams will engage in a greater frequency of RHIE bouts than Bottom 4 teams, with shorter
24	                                     recovery periods between consecutive efforts.
25	                                     Study Design: Cohort study.
26	                                     Methods: A total of 104 semi-elite rugby league players from 11 teams wore global positioning system units during 28
27	                                     Queensland Cup rugby league matches. Recovery between efforts was classified as <10, 11 to 20, 21 to 30, 31 to 60, and 61
28	                                     to 120 seconds.
29	                                     Results: The majority of RHIE bouts were performed with ≤10 seconds recovery between efforts for both Top 4 and
30	                                     Bottom 4 teams. Top 4 teams performed a greater proportion of RHIE bouts with ≤10 seconds recovery between efforts than
31	                                     Bottom 4 teams (effect size [ES], 0.27 ± 0.19), while only trivial differences (ES, 0.17 ± 0.20) were found between Top 4 and
32	                                     Bottom 4 teams for the proportion of RHIE with 61 to 120 seconds recovery between efforts. Wide-running forwards from
33	                                     Top 4 teams performed a greater proportion of RHIE bouts with ≤10 seconds recovery between efforts (ES, 0.59 ± 0.40) and
34	                                     a smaller proportion of RHIE bouts with 61 to 120 seconds recovery between efforts (ES, 0.62 ± 0.38) than wide-running
35	                                     forwards from Bottom 4 teams.
36	                                     Conclusion: Rugby league players perform proportionally more RHIE bouts with ≤10 seconds recovery between efforts
37	                                     than any other recovery duration. In addition, Top 4 teams are more likely to complete a greater proportion of short (≤10
38	                                     seconds) recovery RHIE bouts than Bottom 4 teams.
39	                                     Clinical Relevance: These findings demonstrate the demanding nature of RHIE activity in rugby league. To be successful,
40	                                     teams should train for these demanding passages of play.
41	                                     Keywords: collision sport; global positioning system; match analysis; team sports

                                     The “Worst-Case Scenario”: Recovery
                                     Between Repeated High-Intensity Efforts
                                     in Rugby League Match-Play
                                     Tim J. Gabbett, BHSc (Hons), PhD*†‡§


                                     Background: Repeated high-intensity effort (RHIE) activity is known to be a critical component of high-intensity,
                                     intermittent team sports. Despite the importance of this quality, there are few studies comparing the RHIE activity of higher-
                                     and lower-ranked teams competing in the same competition. This study characterized the distribution of recovery times
                                     between RHIE in Top 4 and Bottom 4 semi-elite rugby league players.
                                     Hypothesis: Players from Top 4 teams will engage in a greater frequency of RHIE bouts than Bottom 4 teams, with shorter
                                     recovery periods between consecutive efforts.
                                     Study Design: Cohort study.
                                     Methods: A total of 104 semi-elite rugby league players from 11 teams wore global positioning system units during 28
                                     Queensland Cup rugby league matches. Recovery between efforts was classified as <10, 11 to 20, 21 to 30, 31 to 60, and 61
                                     to 120 seconds.
                                     Results: The majority of RHIE bouts were performed with ≤10 seconds recovery between efforts for both Top 4 and
                                     Bottom 4 teams. Top 4 teams performed a greater proportion of RHIE bouts with ≤10 seconds recovery between efforts than
                                     Bottom 4 teams (effect size [ES], 0.27 ± 0.19), while only trivial differences (ES, 0.17 ± 0.20) were found between Top 4 and
                                     Bottom 4 teams for the proportion of RHIE with 61 to 120 seconds recovery between efforts. Wide-running forwards from
                                     Top 4 teams performed a greater proportion of RHIE bouts with ≤10 seconds recovery between efforts (ES, 0.59 ± 0.40) and
                                     a smaller proportion of RHIE bouts with 61 to 120 seconds recovery between efforts (ES, 0.62 ± 0.38) than wide-running
                                     forwards from Bottom 4 teams.
                                     Conclusion: Rugby league players perform proportionally more RHIE bouts with ≤10 seconds recovery between efforts
                                     than any other recovery duration. In addition, Top 4 teams are more likely to complete a greater proportion of short (≤10
                                     seconds) recovery RHIE bouts than Bottom 4 teams.
                                     Clinical Relevance: These findings demonstrate the demanding nature of RHIE activity in rugby league. To be successful,
                                     teams should train for these demanding passages of play.
                                     Keywords: collision sport; global positioning system; match analysis; team sports

Article history:                                        Objectives: Recurrent ankle sprains can be reduced by a neuromuscular training program (NMT). The way
Received 28 April 2016                                  NMT is delivered may inﬂuence the incidence of long term recurrent injuries, residual pain and disability.
Received in revised form                                Design: This RCT with a follow-up of twelve months, evaluated whether the implementation method of a
19 November 2016
                                                        proven effective NMT program delivered by a mobile application or a written instruction booklet, resulted
Accepted 3 December 2016
                                                        in differences in injury incidence rates, functional ankle disability/pain in the long term, assuming equal
Available online 9 December 2016

                                                        Methods: 220 athletes with a history of ankle sprain were recruited for this RCT. 110 athletes were offered
Keywords:
Injury prevention
                                                        the freely available “Strengthen your ankle App” and the other 110 received a printed Booklet. Primary
Ankle injury                                            outcome measure was incidence density of ankle sprains. Secondary outcome measures were residual
E-health                                                pain/disability and the individual cumulative number of ankle sprains during follow-up.
                                                        Results: The incidence densities of self-reported ankle sprain recurrences were not signiﬁcantly different
                                                        between both groups (HR 1.06; 95% CI 0.76–1.49). Median FADI (Functional Ankle and Disability Index)
                                                        scores increased equally over time in both groups, indicating a lower rate of limitation and pain in both
                                                        groups at follow-up. Neither FADI scores nor cumulative recurrent injuries were signiﬁcantly different
                                                        between groups.
                                                        Conclusions: This study showed that the implementation method of a NMT program by using an App or a
                                                        Booklet did neither lead to different injury incidence rates in the long term nor did it inﬂuence residual
                                                        functional disability/pain. Assuming equal compliance during the 8-week intervention, both methods
                                                        show similar effectiveness in twelve-month follow-up.
